title: Ninja Assassin
full_review:
When the first beheading occurs before the title comes on the screen, you know you're in ninja land. And indeed, the manic violence of the thinly plotted "Ninja Assassin" (Warner Bros.) -- despite its almost comic resemblance to an extended "Itchy and Scratchy" cartoon from "The Simpsons" -- is both excessive and offensive.

Director James McTeigue ("V for Vendetta") and screenwriters Matthew Sand and J. Michael Straczynski ramp up the spatter factor with extended ballets of special-effects-laden martial-arts battles using expertly flung weaponry that send heads, hands, arms and legs rolling around as if in a sausage factory.

The real aim here is to show off the muscular form and soulful glances of Korean pop star Rain (aka Jeong Ji Hoon) who plays Raizo, an orphan trained from childhood to become a stone-cold killer for hire as part of the secret Ozonu Clan. Having had moments of kindness from a girl during his rigorously heartless training, and seeing her executed for attempting to escape, Raizo breaks with the gang.

In Germany, Mika (Naomie Harris), an agent with something called Europol, is unraveling a string of political assassinations. She's figured out that the Ozonu Clan is behind them, but Raizo gets there just in time to guide her to safety before his former comrades start popping out of the shadows and dropping from ceilings with their sharp-edged mayhem.

When he's not too busy peering from beneath his silky locks, Raizo, needless to say, proves the best fighter of them all.

In return for being saved from puncture wounds and worse, Mika is always conveniently around to drive Raizo away from the swarming ninja, untie him or sneak up on a bad guy.

The assassination subplot is left hanging as a result of the emphasis on strobe-lit butchery by masked men, Raizo's revenge and ninja lore. Who knew, for instance, that ninjas can heal themselves just by concentration? This form of positive thinking keeps Raizo out of the emergency room and on the go to the next showdown. Convenient, that!

The film contains pervasive violence, with mutilation, stabbings and gunplay, frequent bloody and grisly images and some rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
